1:
The book turns a corner, and the witnesses linger first over the vague hinge that opens it. The reformed John Gill takes "after these things" to point back over the finishing of the temple, its dedication, and the keeping of the passover recorded in the previous chapter. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch warn that the formula fixes nothing precisely: it loosely couples what follows to former events without any exact chronological note, just as it does at Genesis 15:1 and Genesis 22:1. They summarise the whole movement it introduces: in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, Ezra the priest and scribe returned from Babylon with a band of priests, Levites, and Israelites, armed with a royal commission to order the worship of God and the observance of the law. The two chronologers who venture a figure disagree by a decade. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following Calmet, sets the seventh year at about sixty-eight years after Cyrus sent back Zerubbabel; the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reckons it fifty-seven years after the events just closed, and places the untold interval between the chapters within the story of the Book of Esther.

Attention then fastens on the man and his fathers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees in Ezra's very priesthood a design of grace: God chose one of the sons of Aaron to be his instrument, that he might put honour upon a priesthood whose glory the captivity had so long eclipsed. Ezra is called "the son of Seraiah," whom Henry and Ellicott take for the eminent high priest who last ministered in Solomon's temple and was slain by the king of Babylon at Riblah, as 2 Kings 25:18 records. But that identification forces a difficulty the witnesses feel keenly. Clarke computes that if Seraiah were Ezra's literal father, Ezra must now be at least a hundred and twenty-two years old; the thing is impossible, and "son" must mean descendant. Henry agrees that at the shortest reckoning some seventy-five years had passed since Seraiah died, and many make it longer, so that Seraiah was not his immediate parent but the first eminent name that met the compiler as he traced the line upward. John Wesley says it plainly: "the son" is the grandson, with divers persons omitted for brevity's sake. The voices converge. A priest of the highest blood, drawn out of exile at the appointed hour, is set before us by a genealogy that honours his descent without pretending to count every link, and that means, in Henry's reading, to restore to the priesthood an honour the exile had stripped away.
6:
"A ready scribe in the law of Moses" becomes the witnesses' occasion to define the office that would shape post-exilic Judaism, and they are unanimous that it means far more than a fair hand. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the Hebrew: sopher machir does not signify a speedy writer or an excellent penman, but one eminently skilful in expounding the law; the same weight, he notes, attaches to the word "scribe" throughout the New Testament, and the Syriac renders it "a wise scribe," an interpreter. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears behind it the "ready writer" of Psalms 45:1, and observes that although Ezra was a priest, and the priestly title is set first in the verses that follow, here at his first appearance in history the compiler chooses the name that expresses his pre-eminent function, the guarding and interpreting of the law he will describe more fully at v.10.

On the man's learning the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and John Wesley preserve an old and striking tradition. Learning had run low among the Jews in Babylon, Henry says, but Ezra was raised up to revive it; the Jews report that he collected and collated all the copies of the law he could find and published an accurate edition of it, together with the prophetical, historical, and poetical books given by divine inspiration, so making up the canon of the Old Testament. If God indeed qualified him for such a work, Henry adds, all generations have reason to call him blessed. Wesley, echoing the same account, sets him beside the lawgiver: Moses in Egypt and Ezra in Babylon, both in the land of their captivity, were wonderfully fitted for eminent service to the church.

Two further notes the witnesses will not pass by. The reformed John Gill marks that this was Ezra's second going up from Babylon, distinct from the first return under Zerubbabel. And all of them dwell on the verse's closing clause. The king granted him all his request — a promise, Ellicott observes, that anticipates the letter copied out at v.11 — yet the true cause lay higher: it was "according to the hand of the LORD his God upon him." Henry makes it the moral of the whole expedition. Every creature is to us what God makes it to be, and from him our judgment proceeds; as we must see the events that befall us in the hand of God, so we must see the hand of God in the events that occur, and acknowledge him with thankfulness when we have reason to call it his good hand. Ellicott adds only that this is the standing formula, dear to Ezra and to Nehemiah alike, for that special providence which watches over the servants of God.
7:
A second company gathers behind Ezra, and the witnesses read the roll of those who joined him — "some of the children of Israel, and of the priests, and the Levites, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinim." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the force of that "some": the Hebrew particle is partitive, a part taken out of the whole, so that what went up was not a nation but a remnant of every order — laymen of Israel and, ranked beneath them, the several grades of temple servants, singers and gatekeepers and the given ones who did the lower work of the house. That these travelled in Ezra's train, they add, is plain from the context and is stated outright both in the royal edict of v.13 and in the fuller account of the journey at v.28.

The reformed John Gill widens the company and probes its motives. Among "the children of Israel" he is willing to reckon some of the ten tribes as well as men of Judah and Benjamin — a hint that the return was not narrowly of the southern exiles only. And he asks why such people had lingered so long. They had stayed behind, he judges, notwithstanding the decree of Cyrus, choosing to remain in Babylon and its provinces until they should see how matters would settle in Judea; now, hearing that the temple was at last finished, that the earlier returners had built themselves houses in their cities and were prospering, they thought it safe and good to go up too. The delay was caution; the going up was confidence rewarded.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the same fact into a tribute to the man they followed. It was a mark of the honour God had put on Ezra, he says, that when he went so many went with him: they had no heart to stay in Babylon once he had left it, and they would venture to dwell in Jerusalem now that he had gone thither. A good and useful man draws others after him; his people loved and trusted him enough to cast in their fortunes with his company and his God. So the witnesses let the bare list carry its quiet weight. The seventh year of Artaxerxes gathers up a fresh migration — priests to serve, Levites and singers and porters to fill out the ordered worship of the house, and ordinary Israelites glad to throw in their lot with a scribe whose God, they had reason to believe, would bring them safely home. What the decree of Cyrus had first opened, the finished temple and a trusted leader now made attractive, and the second wave sets out.
8:
The dating is doubled, and the witnesses count the months carefully. Ezra "came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king," and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott insists that these repeated notes of time must be marked: the arrival is set down here, though the journey itself will be narrated afterwards, for it is the manner of this book to summarise a company and its coming beforehand and then to fill in the story. Laid beside the next verse, the two dates fix the length of the march. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke does the arithmetic: since the caravan set out on the first day of the first month and did not reach the city until the fifth, they were upwards of four months on the road.

Why so long, for a distance that need not have taken half that time? Clarke answers from the make-up of the company. They could not travel fast, being a great multitude that included the aged and the infirm, besides crowds of women and children; and they seem, moreover, to have taken a circuitous route, a point he ties to the later account of the crossing at the river in Ezra 8:24 and following. It was a slow, vulnerable procession, not a swift embassy, and the four months measure the patience the journey required.

The reformed John Gill adds the calendar, placing the fifth month in high summer, answering to part of July and part of August — the height of the dry season, when the roads would at least be passable for so mixed a train. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, gathering this verse with those around it, simply hold the framework steady: the first day of the first month for the setting out, the first day of the fifth for the arrival, the whole journey compassed "according to the good hand of his God upon him," which the following verse will make explicit. The witnesses do not divide; they let the two dates and the four months between them do their proper work. A company too weak to hurry, carrying the vessels and the offerings of the house of God through hostile country, comes safely up in the appointed season — and the safety, all of them insist, is to be read not from the strength of the travellers but from the hand that watched over them the whole way. The bare notice of the fifth month thus already leans toward the confession of providence that verse nine will openly make.
9:
The setting out is dated to the very first day of the very first month, and the witnesses find in that a fitness they do not let pass. The reformed John Gill names the day: this was Nisan, answering to part of March and part of April, and the first of it was the Jewish New Year's day — so that the great pilgrimage began, as it were, with the turning of the year, a fresh start stamped upon the calendar itself. From that day to the first of the fifth month the caravan was on the road, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the framework plain: departure on the first of the first month, arrival on the first of the fifth, the whole compassed "according to the good hand of his God upon him."

It is that closing clause the witnesses most wish to weigh, for it is the heartbeat of the whole narrative. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it up with the earlier notice of the king's favour: Ezra obtained his commission from his prince, and his safe and prosperous journey from God, alike "by the good hand of the Lord that was upon him." It was strange, Henry reflects, that such a man stayed so long in Babylon after his brethren had gone up; but God did not send him thither until he had work for him to do there, and none went but those whose spirits God raised to go. The lesson he draws is the book's own: every creature is that to us which God makes it to be, and from him our judgment proceeds; as we must see the events that befall us in the hand of God, so we must see the hand of God in the events that occur, and acknowledge him with thankfulness when we have reason to call it his good hand.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had already fixed the phrase as a settled formula — the full expression for that special providence over God's servants which both Ezra and Nehemiah loved to own. The witnesses converge without a quarrel. A journey of four months through open and dangerous country, undertaken by a slow and encumbered multitude and burdened with the treasures of the temple, arrives whole and unhurt; and the historian, who might have boasted of Ezra's prudence or the king's protection, traces the safety wholly to the good hand of God. The New Year's departure and the summer's safe arrival are bound together by that one confession, and it will sound again, in Ezra's own mouth, before the chapter closes.
10:
Here the witnesses find the portrait of the man drawn to the life, and they dwell on it with evident affection. "Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments" — and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke opens the first verb: he fixed, purposed, determined, with his heart, with all his powers and affections, to seek the law of God and to do it himself, that he might be properly qualified to teach its statutes and judgments to Israel. The reformed John Gill fills in the seeking: Ezra set his heart to attain the knowledge of the law, to become master of it and expert in it, to know what was forbidden and what required; he bent his studies that way and took great pains, reading, searching, and meditating.

The order of the clauses is, to the witnesses, the very anatomy of a faithful teacher. John Wesley marks it as most observable: first Ezra laboured to understand God's word — and that not for curiosity or ostentation, but in order to practise; next he conscientiously practised what he understood, which made his doctrine far more effectual; and only then did he earnestly seek to instruct others, that they too might know and do it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott traces the same threefold movement — study, then obedience, then the teaching of positive ordinances and moral precepts alike — and calls it a perfect description of a teacher in the congregation. He adds a fine theological caution: the providence of God over Ezra, recorded just before, stands not as the reward of his preparing his heart but as the very reason of it; it was God's good hand that first inclined the heart it then prospered.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a rule for every minister and student of Scripture. Ezra chose the law of the Lord for his study, though bred among the Chaldeans, who were famed for their learning and their star-gazing; he got over the temptation, and the law of his God was more to him than all the writings of their magicians and astrologers, which he knew enough of to despise. He sought the law, made conscience of doing according to it, and set himself to teach Israel — but always in that method: he first learned and then taught, sought the law of the Lord and so laid up a good treasure, and then instructed others and laid out what he had laid up; he also first did and then taught, so that his example confirmed his doctrine. The witnesses do not divide; they leave the verse as the standing measure of a scribe whose knowledge served his obedience, and whose obedience gave weight to his teaching.
11:
With the letter now copied out, the witnesses pause over its heading and over the title by which the king addresses the man. The reformed John Gill notes that "the priest" is justly set before "the scribe," since Ezra was the son of a high priest and lineally descended from Aaron; but the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the other title as the weightier here. In Ezra's case, he says, the function of scribe was more important than that of priest. The word had first meant the writer or copier of the law; by now it meant its expositor — of the general moral commandments and of the special ceremonial statutes alike, and it was chiefly with the latter that this commission had to do. John Wesley finds the same double office in the verse's own phrase, "the words of the commandments": the expression is emphatic, marking that Ezra explained both the words and the things; for the Jews in their captivity had largely lost both the language and the knowledge of God's commands, and Ezra and his companions had to instruct them in both.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry steps back to survey the whole grant the heading introduces, and finds it very ample and full, and beyond what could have been expected. He cannot let its opening style pass without a caution: the emperor writes as "King of kings," a title too high for any mortal to assume, for though he was king of some kings, to speak as if he were king of all is to usurp the prerogative of him who alone has all power in heaven and earth. Yet Henry marks with delight the name the king gives Ezra in the next breath — "a scribe of the law of the God of heaven," a title Ezra plainly valued above every other, reckoning it more his honour to be a scribe of God's law than to be a prince or peer of the empire.

Behind the formal "copy of the letter" the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear the administrative language of the Persian chancery, the same technical terms for copy and letter already met in the correspondence of Ezra 4:11 and Ezra 4:7, and they note that the whole document from here to its close is preserved in its original Aramaic. The witnesses thus prepare the reader for what follows: not a private favour but a formal decree, addressed by the greatest heathen power of the age to a priest who wore, more gladly than any court honour, the name of scribe of the law of his God — and who would use the vast commission, article by article, for the ordering of that God's worship in Jerusalem.
12:
The letter's salutation draws the witnesses to the great title "king of kings," and they weigh how much truth and how much pride it carries. The reformed John Gill will not dismiss it as mere eastern bombast: after Cyrus the Persian monarchs were in fact overlords of many subject kings, and the style was more than boast. He recalls that Cyrus was said to bear it even on his tomb — "Here I lie, Cyrus, king of kings" — and that the Greeks used it too, calling Agamemnon king of kings as the general under whom the other kings fought at Troy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the philology: "Artaxerxes" is the Persian Artachshatra, the Hebrew Artachshasta, and the Persian monarchs had inherited the title "king of kings" from the Babylonians, as Daniel 2:37 already shows. He observes, tellingly, that the historian never applies the grand style to the king; it is used only by the king of himself.

On Ezra's own designation the witnesses hear an honour. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch wrestle with the odd word that qualifies "scribe of the law of the God of heaven," taking it adverbially — "the perfect scribe," the scribe skilled to perfection — and note that the Vulgate rendered it doctissimo, most learned. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the shift of tongue: from this verse to v.26 the letter stands in Aramaic, the language of the empire's business, and the royal name would run in Persian as Ardsheer shahinshah, supreme king, emperor.

The closing words of greeting resist the witnesses more than any title. "Perfect peace, and at such a time," our version reads; but Ellicott confesses the Hebrew is difficult, running literally only "perfect, and so forth," an expression found nowhere else. Our translators, he says, followed the apocryphal Esdras and supplied a salutation, which on the whole is to be accepted — a formal wish of well-being to open a formal decree. Keil notes that the commission proper begins at once, with the order that all Israelites minded to go up to Jerusalem should depart in Ezra's company. So the witnesses set the stage: a heathen emperor, truly and not merely by flattery the king of many kings, opens his firman with a courteous greeting to a Jewish priest whom he honours as the perfect scribe of the God of heaven — the God whose law that emperor is about to command his own officers to uphold.
13:
The commission opens with a grant of liberty, and the witnesses catch both its legal force and its gentleness. The reformed John Gill fastens on the opening words: when the king says "I make a decree," he speaks in the manner of the laws of the Medes and Persians, which, once signed, might not be changed — so that what Ezra carries is not a revocable favour but an irreversible charter. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks what the decree first secures: leave for Ezra to go up to Jerusalem, and for as many of his countrymen as pleased to go up with him. They were captives, Henry reminds us, and could not quit the king's dominions without his royal license; the first article of the grant is simply the open door.

Yet the door is one no one is driven through. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the phrase "of their own freewill": none shall be forced either to go or to stay. The emperor lays no compulsion on any; the whole matter is left to the heart. And Clarke turns it at once into a probe of the reader's own: he who loves his God, he says, will avail himself of this favourable opportunity. The measure of a man's devotion is what he does with an open door that he is not compelled to enter.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the terms precise. The permission runs to "all they of the people of Israel, and of his priests and Levites," that is, to laity and clergy alike within the realm, on the single condition of a willing mind; and those who so choose are to "go with thee" — to travel, that is, in Ezra's company and under his charge, which is why the second wave of returners is everywhere spoken of as gathered around him. The witnesses do not divide, and together they draw out the strange grace of the moment. A pagan king, master of an empire, uses his absolute authority not to conscript but to release; he throws open the road to Jerusalem and leaves it to the love of each exile whether to take it. What Cyrus had begun, Artaxerxes here renews and enlarges, and the historian lets the freedom of the offer test the faith of the people. Those who go will go because they would rather worship the God of Israel in his own land than sit at ease in Babylon — and the decree, unalterable as the law of Persia, guarantees that their choice shall stand.
14:
Two things in this clause draw the witnesses' comment: the body that sends Ezra, and the rule by which he is to act. On the first, the reformed John Gill explains the number: the kings of Persia kept seven counsellors from the days of Darius Hystaspis, who had himself been chosen out of seven nobles to be king, and ever after the seven held a privileged place at the throne — so that it was no small honour that Ezra was sent with a commission from the king and his seven counsellors together. The grammatical-historical witnesses fill in the history. Keil and Delitzsch identify the seven as the supreme court of the realm, and point, as does Charles Ellicott, to their appearance in Esther 1:14; Ellicott adds that they were probably the heads of those families who had aided Darius against the false Smerdis, as Herodotus tells the tale, while the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes that the names of the seven may be gathered from Esther 1:10.

The errand itself is an enquiry. Ezra is "sent to inquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem," and the witnesses read this as no idle survey. Keil and Delitzsch take it to mean an investigation into the religious and civil condition of the Jewish community, in order to arrange its affairs in conformity with the law of God. John Wesley puts it sharply: Ezra was to make inquiry into all abuses and deviations from the law, and to redress them — a commission of reform, not of mere inspection. Ellicott agrees that the first charge was to examine the state of city and province precisely with regard to the relation of both to the divine law.

And that law is the standard the clause names last and the witnesses weigh most: "according to the law of thy God which is in thine hand." Wesley dwells on the phrase — the law was in Ezra's hand as the matter of his daily study, now and always, so that he carried it not as a stranger might carry an unread statute but as its lifelong scholar. Ellicott and Keil take "in thy hand" to mean simply that Ezra possessed and understood it; it was the rule he handled and lived by. The witnesses converge on the wonder of it: a heathen court commissions a Jewish scribe to set the province of Judah in order, and names as the measure of that order not the king's pleasure but the God of Israel's own law — the very law Ezra had prepared his heart to seek, to do, and to teach.
15:
The commission now turns to money, and the witnesses trace where it came from and what it says. The gift named first is the freewill offering of the king and his counsellors themselves, "unto the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem." The reformed John Gill takes it for a voluntary contribution made by the emperor and his nobles toward the service of the temple — whether for procuring vessels that were wanting or for the sacrifices to be offered there — with which Ezra was now entrusted and sent. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sort the whole benefaction into three streams, of which this is the first: the gifts of the king and his counsellors; then the gold and silver Ezra should gather throughout the province of Babylon, being empowered to collect even among its heathen inhabitants; and lastly the freewill offerings of his own countrymen. Three fountains, from the crown, from the Gentiles, and from the exiles, all flowing toward the one house at Jerusalem.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the fact into a threefold reflection. It redounds first to the honour of God as the one living and true God, for here even men who worshipped other gods were so far convinced of his sovereignty that they were willing to be at charges to recommend themselves to his favour — much as the psalmist foresaw the daughter of Tyre courting the king with a gift and the rich among the people entreating his favour in Psalms 45:12. It redounds, second, to the praise of this heathen prince, that he honoured the God of Israel though his worshippers were a despised handful, poor and unable to bear the charges of their own religion, and though he himself was never won to quit his own superstition; he protected and encouraged the Jews, and did not merely bid them be warmed and filled but gave them the things they needed.

And it redounds, third, to the reproach of the wicked kings of Judah. Those who had been bred in the knowledge and worship of the God of Israel, who had his law and his prophets, had again and again plundered and impoverished the temple; and here a heathen king enriches it. Henry hears in the reversal a foreshadowing of a greater one — the gospel afterward rejected by many of the Jews and welcomed by the Gentiles. The witnesses do not divide. They let the king's silver and gold preach a double sermon: the reach of God's honour among the nations, and the shame of a covenant people outdone in zeal for God's house by the very heathen they despised.
16:
A single word in this verse — "find" — could be dangerously misread, and the witnesses hasten to guard it. When the king empowers Ezra to take "all the silver and gold that thou canst find in all the province of Babylon," the reformed John Gill insists this is no license to seize property wherever it lay, whether the owners were willing or not. Following the Jewish commentator Jarchi, he explains that Ezra might take only what was freely offered — whatever he could gather in that way, and no more. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reaches the same sense by tracing the verb: to find here is to procure, in the way the word is used when Noah "found grace in the eyes of the LORD" at Genesis 6:8; it means whatever Ezra could get of the king's subjects by way of free gift, not by exaction. Adam Clarke confirms the point from the flow of the commission: the king and his counsellors had already made their present, and Ezra is now simply authorised to receive whatever further contribution any inhabitant of the province of Babylon might think proper to give.

The generosity thus reached beyond the exiles. The gift is joined here "with the freewill offering of the people and of the priests, offering willingly for the house of their God" — and while Wesley takes "the people" to mean the people of Israel, the witnesses agree with Keil and Delitzsch that the wider collection swept in Gentile and Jewish givers alike, all that Ezra could raise across the whole satrapy. The stress everywhere falls on the willingness: nothing wrung, all bestowed; a heathen province opening its hand toward a temple most of its inhabitants would never see.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the phrase that closes the verse and will keep recurring — "which is in Jerusalem." The repetition, he observes, is partly the manner of the literature of this period, which loves such fixed formulas; but here, as in some other places, it carries more than habit. It implies a deep reverence, a lingering over the one spot on earth where the God of heaven had set his name. The witnesses do not divide. They leave the verse as a portrait of open-handed devotion rightly understood: Ezra goes not as a tax-gatherer with power to distrain, but as the trusted steward of a river of free gifts, drawn from crown and commoner, Jew and Gentile, and all of it flowing with reverence toward the house of God in Jerusalem.
17:
The first and chief use of all this treasure is now specified, and the witnesses note both the object and a curious mark of authorship. The money is to buy, and to buy speedily, the victims of sacrifice — "bullocks, rams, lambs, with their meat offerings and their drink offerings" — to be presented on the altar of the house of God in Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the order as one of priority: Ezra is to provide first of all for the sacrificial ceremonial, before any lesser expense. And he explains why the grain and wine are named alongside the animals: every sacrifice had its own appointed meat-offering and drink-offering, according to the standing rule laid down in Numbers 15, so that to buy the beasts was necessarily to buy the flour, oil, and wine that must go up with them.

Here Ellicott makes an acute observation about the shape of the document. Such minute liturgical phrases as these — the pairing of meat- and drink-offerings, the exact list of victims — could hardly have come from a Persian chancery of themselves; they are, he judges, the very words Ezra dictated into his own commission. The heathen king lent his seal and his treasury, but the priest supplied the detail, so that the decree speaks with a precision only a scribe of the law could have furnished. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same logic in the connecting particle: for this very reason — because the silver had been furnished by king, counsellors, and the heathen and Israelite givers of Babylon alike — Ezra is diligently to lay it out on the sacrifices and to offer them upon the altar.

The reformed John Gill and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keep the emphasis practical. Gill marks only that the buying is done "with this money," the sum so freely contributed from every quarter; Henry, surveying the article, notes that Ezra was trusted to lay out the money in the sacrifices to be offered on God's altar. The witnesses do not divide, and the verse leaves a striking picture. A pagan emperor's gold is turned, at a Jewish priest's own direction, into the ordered worship of Israel's God — bullocks and rams and lambs bought in haste and burned on the restored altar, each with its measured portion of flour and wine, exactly as the law of Moses had prescribed centuries before. The generosity of Persia is thus made to serve, down to the smallest liturgical particular, the covenant that Persia did not keep.
18:
The commission now does a remarkable thing: it hands the surplus back to Jewish discretion. "Whatsoever shall seem good to thee, and to thy brethren, to do with the rest of the silver and the gold, that do after the will of your God." The reformed John Gill takes "thy brethren" to mean the priests whom Ezra should think fit to take in to his assistance, so that the leftover funds were to be disposed by Ezra and his priestly colleagues together. What strikes the witnesses is the freedom the clause grants and the single limit it sets.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marvels at the liberty: the king gave them the fullest latitude to order everything according to their own institutions, binding them to no form or mode of worship. A pagan monarch, funding a religion not his own, imposes none of his own rites upon it, but leaves its ordering entirely to the law and conscience of its ministers. Yet the liberty is not lawless. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fixes on the governing phrase "after the will of your God," which the king himself set as the rule — the will of God, Henry notes, with which the Jews were far better acquainted than the king was. Let the will of our God, he urges, be always our rule in what we spend, and particularly in what we lay out for his service; God's work must always be done according to God's will.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the practical reach of so open a clause. This grant of large latitude, he says, would be of great importance for the general beautifying of the temple — a purpose Ezra will name with thanksgiving at the chapter's close in v.27. The surplus, that is, was not idle margin but the means by which the house of God might be adorned beyond the bare necessities of sacrifice. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause in the same spirit, as leaving to Ezra and his brethren all further disposal of the money, always under the one condition of the divine will. The witnesses do not divide. They see in the article a rare and generous trust: the empire supplies the wealth, names no ceremony, dictates no design, and requires only that whatever remains be spent as the God of Israel would have it — so that even the freedom of the grant becomes, in the priest's hands, an instrument of reverence.
19:
Alongside the money the king consigns a further gift — the sacred vessels — and the witnesses are chiefly concerned to distinguish these from an earlier consignment and to weigh the solemn phrase that governs their handing over. The reformed John Gill describes them as vessels of silver, basins of gold, and vessels of fine copper, and is careful to say what they were not: these were not the vessels that had formerly belonged to the temple, for those had already been restored, delivered by Cyrus to Sheshbazzar at the first return. These are new gifts, freely offered by the present king and his counsellors at this time. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says the same in a word — the vessels were offered to be added to those Zerubbabel had brought up — and points forward to the inventory of them that Ezra will give when he weighs out the treasure at Ezra 8:25.

Keil and Delitzsch enlarge the list of donors. The gold and silver vessels, they note, were presented by the king and his counsellors, and by the princes, and by all Israel — a benefaction as broad as the offering of money, gathered from crown and court and commoner alike. And they attend closely to the charge laid upon Ezra concerning them: he is to "deliver" them "before the God of Jerusalem." The verb, they explain, is one of completion — to make full, hence to hand over entirely, to consign — so that Ezra's task is not merely to carry the vessels but faithfully to render them up, whole and complete, at their destination. The phrase "before the God of Jerusalem" they take as a compressed form for the God whose dwelling is at Jerusalem, the place where he had set his name.

The witnesses do not divide, and the small verse carries a quiet dignity. Ezra is made the trustee of holy things — not the old vessels of Solomon's temple, plundered and then given back, but fresh treasures laid on the altar of a heathen king's liberality. His charge is to bring them the whole long way from Babylon and to consign them, entire and unembezzled, into the service of the house of God. It is the same trust Ezra will discharge with such scrupulous care when he weighs the silver and gold and the vessels into the hands of the priests, counting nothing his own; and the phrase "before the God of Jerusalem" reminds him, and the reader, that every such gift is rendered at last not to a temple only but to the God who dwells there.
20:
Beyond the gifts already gathered, the king opens to Ezra his own treasury for whatever else the work might require. "Whatsoever more shall be needful for the house of thy God, which thou shalt have occasion to bestow, bestow it out of the king's treasure house." The reformed John Gill understands the clause of further expenses for the beautifying and adorning of the temple — costs that could not be reckoned in advance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as an open provision for the unforeseen: whatever necessary charges should arise which the contributions in hand could not meet, Ezra was to defray out of the royal treasury, and to that end the king would command all the treasurers on this side the river to furnish whatever Ezra should require.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry admires the wisdom and warmth of the arrangement. It was considerately done: Ezra, having yet to enquire into the state of things, could not know what he would need, and was modest in his demands, so the king in effect drew him a standing warrant upon the royal revenues, to furnish what he should have occasion for and place it to the king's account. And it was kindly done, Henry adds, evincing a great affection for the temple and a great confidence in Ezra. It is the interest of princes and great men, he reflects, to use their wealth and power for the support of religion; what else are great revenues good for, but that they enable men to do much good, if they have but hearts to do it?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott grounds the clause in Persian administration: every satrap had his local treasury, on which such a draft could be drawn. He grants that the decree here gives Ezra very large powers indeed — yet he notes, with the historian's eye, that the following verses will add a measure of qualification, a ceiling upon the open grant. Keil and Delitzsch mark the emphatic turn of the king's speech as he presses toward that royal order, the doubled "I, even I." The witnesses do not divide. They see a heathen king pledging his own treasury, without limit named in this verse, to the beautifying of a God he did not worship, and trusting the whole draft to a single Jewish priest — a confidence so extravagant that the next verse must temper it with figures, lest the powers granted outrun even a Persian king's intent. The generosity is real; the caution that follows only shows how great the generosity had been.
21:
The king now turns from Ezra to his own officers and issues the order that backs the warrant. The reformed John Gill identifies the men addressed: "the treasurers which are beyond the river" are the receivers of the royal tribute, tax, and custom in the vast province west of the Euphrates, toward the land of Israel — the very officials through whose hands the taxes of Judea passed. To all of them the decree goes out that whatever Ezra should require of them was to be done, and done speedily.

The witnesses hear in the verse's opening a deliberate weight. The king writes "I, even I Artaxerxes the king," and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark it as an emphatic royal self-assertion — the full authority of the throne set behind the order, so that no treasurer might treat Ezra's requisitions as a private request to be delayed or questioned. What the perfect scribe asked, the empire's revenue was to supply, and promptly. Not less telling is the title the king gives Ezra as he commands his own tax-gatherers to obey him: "Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven." Through the chapter the pagan monarch honours that name; here he sets it as the credential by which his treasurers are to recognise the man whose word they must fulfil.

So the scribe of a foreign God's law is made, by imperial decree, a claimant upon the Persian treasury throughout the western satrapy. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott alike observe that the command runs straight on into the schedule of the next verse, where the open draft of v.20 is at once given its measure — so many talents of silver, so much wheat and wine and oil — the very qualification Ellicott had foretold. The witnesses do not divide. They leave the verse as the hinge between promise and provision: the king's absolute "I, even I" guarantees the grant, names Ezra by the title he most valued, binds every treasurer beyond the river to swift obedience, and then, in the same breath, prepares to set the bounds that keep even so lavish a bounty within reason. Royal will and administrative order meet, and both are bent to the service of the house of God, so that the officers who gathered Judea's taxes are turned into stewards of Judea's worship. Gill's small note on the geography quietly underlines the marvel: it was in the western province, on the very border of the land of Israel, that the empire's revenue was now placed at a Jewish scribe's disposal, and its own collectors bound to honour his word.
22:
The open draft is here given its bounds, and the witnesses turn arithmetician to reckon what the ceiling meant. The treasurers are to supply Ezra up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred measures of wheat, a hundred baths of wine and of oil, "and salt without prescribing how much." The reformed John Gill values the silver at some thirty-five thousand pounds, and notes on Jarchi's authority that it was chiefly meant for the buying of the offerings. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the several measures their content: the measure of wheat is the cor, a little more than seventy-five gallons; the bath of wine holds some seven gallons and more; so that the schedule, generous as it looks, was a definite reckoning of grain and drink and precious metal.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the paradox of the figure. A restriction is certainly laid upon the amount, he says — the open promise of the former verse is now capped — yet the restriction is so large as to seem almost indefinite, the silver alone perhaps reaching four-and-twenty thousand pounds. And he sets the grant against the land it would draw upon: Palestine abounded in just these products, wheat and wine and oil, which were regularly remitted to the king's service as the revenue of the province; salt especially was plentiful near the Dead Sea, which is doubtless why of salt alone the king names no limit, bidding his officers supply it without measure. Keil and Delitzsch add the philological note that the cor here named is the later word for the older chomer, the great dry measure of 1 Kings 5:2 and Ezekiel 45:14, equal to ten ephahs or baths.

The witnesses do not divide, and the schedule tells its own story. The king's bounty is vast but not reckless: he sets a ceiling high enough to meet every need of the altar yet exact enough to protect his treasury from abuse, and he leaves only the cheap and plentiful salt unlimited. That these commodities were the very produce of Judea meant the grant cost the crown little and served the temple much — the taxes of the land, in effect, turned back to the worship of the land's God. Even in the setting of a limit, the witnesses find the same providence that has run through the whole commission: a heathen king's revenue measured out, to the talent and the bath, for the sacrifices of Israel.
23:
The king's charge reaches its most reverent height, and the witnesses gather around his fear of a divine anger. "Whatsoever is commanded by the God of heaven, let it be diligently done for the house of the God of heaven; for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons?" The reformed John Gill grounds the phrase in Scripture: what the God of heaven commands is what he commanded in the law given by Moses, so that the king in effect binds his officers to see the Mosaic ordinances fulfilled. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enters into the royal motive. Artaxerxes seems to have believed himself appointed by the Almighty to this work, and therefore wished it done heartily; for he knew that if it were neglected God would be displeased, and the kingdom might be cut off from him or from his posterity. The dread of heaven's wrath is not a courtier's flourish but the king's own conviction.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks how the language itself betrays that reverence. In this solemn and devout firman the title "the God of heaven" occurs twice over, and the Persian prince openly deprecates the wrath of that God — a striking posture for a pagan emperor toward the deity of a subject people. Ellicott sets the fear in its moment: in this seventh year of Artaxerxes, which he dates to 458 before Christ, the tide of war had turned for Persia against the Athenians in Egypt, so that a king with reason to feel the precariousness of empire might well be anxious to have every heaven on his side.

The closing words, "and his sons," draw a further note. Ellicott observes that though Artaxerxes was still young at this time, he is said to have left eighteen sons — so that his care to avert wrath against the realm and his sons looked to a whole dynasty's security. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the very ground of the lavish authorisation: the diligent doing of God's commands is urged precisely that no wrath may fall upon the king and his house. The witnesses do not divide. They find in the sentence a remarkable confession from a heathen throne — that the God of heaven is a God whose neglected worship brings wrath upon kingdoms, and whose honoured worship secures them. Artaxerxes, unconverted, funds and defends the religion of Israel out of a shrewd and reverent fear; and the historian lets that fear preach what many a king of Judah had refused to learn, that the surest safety of a realm is the honouring of the true God.
24:
A fresh clause frees the whole ministry of the temple from taxation, and the witnesses weigh both its generosity and its reasonableness. "It shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom" upon any of the priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinim, or other ministers of the house of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks how emphatically the exemption is introduced — the freeing of so large a body as the entire temple staff from every kind of impost was no small concession, and the decree announces it with formal solemnity, "we certify you." Keil and Delitzsch note that this too is addressed to the treasurers beyond the river, the levyers of the taxes, forbidding them to lay toll or tribute or custom upon any servant of the house, from the highest order to the lowest.

The reformed John Gill observes that the king shows a right and exact knowledge of the distinct offices and services of these persons — priests to sacrifice, Levites to assist, singers and porters and given ones each to their task — so that the exemption is granted not blindly but with understanding of the whole ordered ministry it covered. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the fairness of it: since these men had no private revenues of their own, living wholly by their sacred service, it would have been unreasonable to lay them under taxation. The privilege, on this reading, was not mere favouritism but justice to a class that possessed nothing to be taxed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the honour and its proper bound. The exemption, reaching from the greatest of the priests to the least of the Nethinim, put a great mark of dignity upon them, making them as free denizens of the empire and gaining them respect as favourites of the crown; and it left them at liberty to attend their ministry with the more cheerfulness and freedom. Yet Henry adds a shrewd qualification: it was only what they needed for themselves and their families and the maintenance of their ministry that was allowed to come to them free of custom; if any of them should abuse the privilege to meddle in trade and merchandise, he justly lost the benefit of it. The witnesses do not divide. They see in the clause a heathen king endowing the servants of Israel's God with a real and understanding kindness — freeing the poor ministers of the altar from every tax, that nothing might hinder them from the worship they existed to maintain, while the exemption stayed tied to the sacred calling that alone had earned it.
25:
The commission's last great grant makes Ezra a magistrate as well as a scribe, and the witnesses trace both the breadth of the power and the wisdom that was to guide it. "Thou, Ezra, after the wisdom of thy God that is in thine hand, set magistrates and judges, which may judge all the people that are beyond the river." The reformed John Gill hears in "the wisdom of thy God that is in thine hand" a double sense — the large share of wisdom Ezra had received from the Lord and could readily use, and, behind it, the law of God itself, framed with the highest wisdom and now held in Ezra's hand as his rule. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees: it is the wisdom God had put into Ezra's heart, made visible in the works of his hand, by which he was to order the judicature of his people.

On the reach of the appointment the witnesses are careful. Read baldly, Ezra is to set judges over "all the people beyond the river"; but Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott alike restrict this by the qualifying clause "all such as know the laws of thy God." The jurisdiction, that is, runs over the Jews, the whole community that professed the religion of Israel throughout the western satrapy — who were thereby granted judges of their own nation, acquainted with the law, and exempted from the heathen magistrates. Ellicott puts it strongly: the firman here returns directly to Ezra and makes him supreme in the province over the Jewish population, with absolute authority in religion.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry counts this the crowning favour of the whole grant. It was no small thing that the Jews should have nobles and judges of themselves, and especially of Ezra's own nomination; all who knew the laws of Ezra's God were brought under their jurisdiction, and the judges were encouraged even to make proselytes, teaching the law to such as did not know it — "and teach ye them that know them not." That closing charge the witnesses read variously but not contrarily: Ellicott takes "them that know them not" for the Jews who had comparatively forsaken the law and needed to be reclaimed to it, while Keil and Delitzsch read the same union of judging and teaching as the double duty of Ezra's new courts. The witnesses do not divide. They see a heathen empire handing a subject people the right to govern themselves by the law of their God, and setting a scribe over them who would both enforce that law upon the knowing and teach it to the ignorant — a measure of self-rule under the divine law such as, Henry marvels, few kings of Judah had ever done more to secure.
26:
The grant of judicial power is armed here with penalties, and the witnesses weigh the sword thus put into Ezra's hand. "Whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him." The reformed John Gill asks who is meant by the offender and gives two answers: it may be the judge who delays justice or fails to execute it according to the law of God and of the king, or, more broadly, the people who refuse to obey — the law of God in matters of religion, and the law of the king in civil things, Judea being now a province of the Persian empire. Some, he adds, take "the law of the king" to mean only this present decree, so that to resist Ezra's commission was itself the punishable crime; and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the law of the king is the edict now given, whose neglect or transgression brought a man to judgment.

On the penalties the witnesses simply spread out the fearful list. Death, banishment, confiscation of goods, imprisonment — almost every species of punishment, says the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, that should be inflicted on culprits in any civilised state. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the word for banishment as a rooting out, an exile that tore a man from his place; and they note that this severity, like the jurisdiction it enforced, fell chiefly upon those who were Israelites born. Clarke marks a further point of interest: with this verse the Aramaic portion of the chapter, in which the whole royal letter stands, comes to its end.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws out how much the clause conferred. Here civil authority is added to religious; and though the Persians commonly entrusted such powers to their provincial administrators, with more or less of reservation, their combination in the one person of this servant of Jehovah was so unusual that it demanded express statement. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley can only wonder at the sum of it: what could David himself, as king, have done more for the honour of God and the furtherance of religion? The witnesses do not divide. They see a heathen emperor arming a Jewish priest with the full power of the state — over life, liberty, and goods — to enforce the law of Israel's God upon Israel's own people; a concentration of civil and sacred authority in one faithful hand so complete that it needed the letter's plainest words to make it credible, and so ample that it rivalled the best that the greatest of Judah's own kings had done for the cause of God.
27:
With the letter fully copied, Ezra breaks into praise, and the witnesses gather warmly around the sudden doxology. "Blessed be the LORD God of our fathers, which hath put such a thing as this in the king's heart." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that Ezra cannot proceed in his story without this thankful acknowledgment; and where a courtier might have written "God save the king," the scribe writes "Blessed be the Lord," for in everything we must give thanks and own God's hand in whatever pleases us. Henry fixes on the marvel that God put such a thing into the king's heart — God can put things into men's hearts, and into their heads too, which would never arise there of themselves, both by his providence and by his grace; if any good appear in our own hearts or in others', we must own that God put it there and bless him for it, for it is he that worketh in us both to will and to do. When princes and magistrates act for the suppression of vice and the encouragement of religion, Henry urges, we must thank God who inclined their hearts, as truly as if they had granted us some private favour.

The witnesses linger too on the word "beautify." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes it as a general term for all that belonged to the restoration of the temple; and he reads the whole ejaculation as the solitary expression of Ezra's private devotion, incorporated into the record so artlessly that it confirms the impression that the entire narrative comes from Ezra's own hand — a sudden burst of thanksgiving that reminds him of Nehemiah's habit of prayer. Henry adds a caution about wherein the true beauty lay: we read of no orders to paint or gild the house or garnish it with precious stones, but to be sure that the ordinances of God were administered there constantly and exactly according to their institution; and that, he says, was indeed the beautifying of the temple.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch measure how much the commission had won. It granted the Jews all they could possibly desire from their heathen rulers for the establishment of their civil and religious polity; Artaxerxes was here not only treading in the steps of Cyrus and Darius but going beyond them, in granting the community a jurisdiction of its own — without which, since Israel's social and religious life were so closely knit, no heathen magistrate, however well-meaning, could have governed them for good. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley say simply that this is Ezra's thanksgiving to God for the whole decree. The witnesses do not divide. They hear a devout scribe trace a pagan king's astonishing generosity to its true source, and bless not the king but the God who moved the king's heart — the God of the fathers, still at work in the counsels of an empire, for the beauty of his house.
28:
The chapter ends where Ezra's heart is fullest — in a confession that all the favour he had found was God's mercy and all his courage God's gift. "And hath extended mercy unto me before the king, and his counsellors, and before all the king's mighty princes." The reformed John Gill spells out the mercy: Ezra had been shown favour before Artaxerxes, his seven counsellors, and the nobles of the realm, in being appointed to carry their freewill offerings to Jerusalem, to bear the king's commands to his treasurers, and to lead up as many of the Jews as were willing to go. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the same point the key to Ezra's humility: the honour done to himself before the whole council of Persia, Ezra ascribes not to his own merit but to the mercy of God.

On the second clause the witnesses dwell longest, for it names the source of Ezra's strength. "I was strengthened as the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, and I gathered together out of Israel chief men to go up with me." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke admires the spirit of it: in all that the king decreed, Ezra saw the hand of God, and therefore gave God the praise and took courage; there is a most amiable piety in the way he simply states the case, tells what the king had determined, and then points beyond it to the true agent of the whole business — the Lord God of his fathers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the humility. The king, no doubt, had an eye to Ezra's own merit and preferred him as a man of sense and worth; but Ezra ascribes his preferment purely to God's mercy, and though he was himself a man of courage, he attributed his encouragement not to his own heart but to God's hand: "I was strengthened," he says, as the hand of the Lord my God was upon me.

John Wesley draws the lesson the verse presses on every reader: if God gives us his hand, we are bold and cheerful; if he withdraw it, we are weak as water; and whatever service we are enabled to do for God and our generation, God must have all the glory of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the strengthened Ezra at once turned his new courage to use, gathering the chief men of Israel to go up with him — the leaders whose enrolment the next chapter will record. The witnesses do not divide. They close the chapter on a scribe who, laden with an emperor's honours and an unheard-of commission, looks past king and counsellors and princes to the mercy that moved them and the hand that upheld him, and takes courage not from his standing at court but from the God whose good hand had been upon him all the way.
2:
The pedigree runs on backward through a chain of famous priestly names — Shallum, Zadok, Ahitub, Amariah, Azariah, Meraioth, Zerahiah, Uzzi, Bukki, Abishua, Phinehas, Eleazar — until it rests at last upon "Aaron the chief priest." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply lay the list out; the interest of the other witnesses falls on how much it silently leaves unsaid. Adam Clarke counts only sixteen generations here between Ezra and Aaron, where the fuller register of 1 Chronicles 6:3 and following gives no fewer than twenty-two; the deficiency, the wesleyan-arminian commentator shows, must be repaired from that chapter, supplying the names dropped between Amariah the son of Meraioth in 1 Chronicles 6:7 and Azariah the son of Johanan in 1 Chronicles 6:10.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the omission under a governing principle rather than treating it as a flaw. Hebrew genealogy, he observes, follows a law by which every ancestor may be called a "father" and every descendant a "son"; the list is given compendiously, as often in Scripture, and the missing links of 1 Chronicles 6 are easily supplied. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and John Wesley say the same in fewer words: the line is carried up as high as Aaron, many names left out for brevity's sake, to be filled in from the priestly register. None of them reads the gaps as error; a genealogy of this kind means to establish descent, not to number every generation.

Yet the witnesses will not let the list become a mere skeleton. The names it keeps are chosen to plant Ezra in the very trunk of the Aaronic house — through Zadok, the priest who stood by David and Solomon, back through Phinehas of the zealous memory, to Eleazar and to Aaron himself. To trace Ezra's blood to the chief priest is to say that the scribe who now comes up from Babylon to restore the law comes with every right of the altar behind him. Henry had already drawn the lesson from the whole descent: that God, in raising up such a man at such a time, was putting fresh honour upon the priesthood the exile had dishonoured, and fitting one man wonderfully, as Moses had been fitted in Egypt, for an eminent service to the church. The line that looks at first like dry catalogue becomes, in the witnesses' hands, the credential of the man God had prepared, and the pledge that the reformation he brings is no innovation but a return to the ancient priestly trust.
